subject: Physics
subtopic: Current electricity, Ohm's law and circuit analysis
axis_note: ladder_position is a curriculum coordinate. It is never a learner estimate, and Core1A/Core1B may not consult one.

must_contain: A boundary in a wire and equal time windows so current is read as charge-per-time.
A series path in which entering and leaving current can be compared.

controlled_variation.vary: the resistor value in one unbranched steady circuit
controlled_variation.hold: the charge flow has no junction and no place for steady charge accumulation
controlled_variation.notice: the current is the same on both sides even though other electrical quantities may change

rungs.aha: Macroscopic current can be produced by a slow average drift of many charge carriers; the response of a circuit is not the travel time of one electron from source to load.
learner_owns: R1: current is charge-per-time and charge is conserved through an unbranched element.
must_contain: The factors n, e, A, and drift speed connected to current as I = n e A v_d.
A separate comparison between carrier drift direction/speed and the propagation of the electrical influence through a circuit.
Current density J as a directed local flow quantity, with J = sigma E only under the stated material model.

misconception.wrong_idea: Electrons switched on at the source race through the whole wire to the lamp at nearly the speed of light.
misconception.diagnostic_prompt: If carrier drift is extremely slow, why can a distant lamp respond almost immediately after the switch closes?
misconception.repair: Separate carrier motion from signal propagation: many carriers already occupy the conductor and begin drifting when the electromagnetic influence reaches them.

rungs.closure: Use I = n e A v_d to explain how a measurable current can coexist with a small drift speed, and distinguish that drift from circuit response propagation.

controlled_variation.vary: carrier number density or wire cross-sectional area
controlled_variation.hold: the same current magnitude and carrier charge
controlled_variation.notice: the required drift speed changes even though the macroscopic current does not

controlled_variation.vary: wire length between switch and lamp
controlled_variation.hold: the conductor type and local drift-speed scale
controlled_variation.notice: the circuit response is not explained by one carrier traversing the full wire

controlled_variation.hold: an ohmic isotropic material at fixed conductivity
controlled_variation.notice: the conventional current-density direction follows E while electron drift is opposite

rungs.aha: Potential difference describes energy transferred per unit charge; a voltage drop is not a loss of charge.
learner_owns: R2: macroscopic current can coexist with slow carrier drift; circuit response is not one electron racing from source to load.
must_contain: The same charge amount moved through two components with different energy changes.
A distinction between charge flow and energy-per-charge.

misconception.wrong_idea: Voltage is the amount of current left after a component.
misconception.diagnostic_prompt: Two series lamps carry the same current but have different voltage drops. What quantity changed across each lamp?
misconception.repair: Keep the current ledger and the energy-per-charge ledger separate: voltage belongs to the second.

rungs.closure: Given equal current through two series components, explain how their voltage drops may differ without charge disappearing.

controlled_variation.vary: the component's energy transfer per coulomb
controlled_variation.hold: the same steady current passes through every component in the series path
controlled_variation.notice: voltage can change while current stays unchanged

must_contain: Pairs of V and I measurements for one element.
A test for whether V/I stays constant as operating point changes.

controlled_variation.vary: applied potential difference across one device
controlled_variation.notice: an ohmic device keeps V/I constant while a non-ohmic device need not

controlled_variation.hold: the device material and measurement method
controlled_variation.notice: the same device can leave the constant-R model when conditions change

rungs.aha: Circuit topology decides which quantity is shared: series elements share current, parallel branches share potential difference.
learner_owns: R4: use V = IR with constant R only when the element is modeled as ohmic under fixed conditions.
must_contain: A node-and-branch picture before any equivalent-resistance arithmetic.
One series comparison and one parallel comparison using the same resistor values.

misconception.wrong_idea: Resistors combine by whichever formula gives the smaller or easier number.
misconception.diagnostic_prompt: Two equal resistors are first placed end-to-end, then across the same two nodes. What stays equal in each arrangement?
misconception.repair: Read the connections first: one path implies shared current; common endpoints imply shared potential difference.

rungs.closure: Given an unlabeled two-resistor connection, identify series or parallel from topology and write the correct equivalent-resistance relation.

controlled_variation.vary: resistor values in one series path
controlled_variation.hold: there is exactly one current path
controlled_variation.notice: the same current passes through each element and voltage divides

controlled_variation.vary: resistor values in two branches sharing both endpoints
controlled_variation.hold: both branches connect to the same two nodes
controlled_variation.notice: the same potential difference appears across both branches and current divides

rungs.aha: Electrical power is the rate of energy transfer, and P = VI can be rewritten using the element model only after the correct V-I relation is established.
learner_owns: R5: topology determines shared current or shared potential difference before combination rules are used.
must_contain: The distinction between energy, energy-per-charge, and energy-per-time.
At least two equivalent power expressions derived from P = VI and V = IR.

misconception.wrong_idea: Using P = V^2/R or P = I^2R is always safe without checking what is held or whether the element is ohmic.
misconception.diagnostic_prompt: Two ohmic resistors are compared once at equal voltage and once at equal current. Which one dissipates more power in each case?
misconception.repair: Start from P = VI; substitute V = IR only after the circuit conditions tell you which quantity is common.

rungs.closure: Choose a valid power expression for a stated circuit condition and predict how dissipation changes when R changes.

controlled_variation.hold: the source maintains the same voltage and elements are modeled ohmically
the current is maintained and elements are modeled ohmically

rungs.aha: Kirchhoff analysis is a conservation ledger: junction equations conserve charge, and signed loop equations conserve energy per charge.
learner_owns: R6: power relations follow from P = VI plus a valid element model and stated circuit conditions.
must_contain: A declared current direction on every branch used in an equation.
A declared traversal direction and sign convention for every loop.

misconception.wrong_idea: A negative solved current means the calculation failed.
misconception.diagnostic_prompt: If an assumed clockwise branch current solves to -0.3 A, what physical direction does that result represent?
misconception.repair: Treat directions as declared references. A negative result reverses the assumed direction; it does not invalidate conservation.

rungs.closure: Write and solve a one-junction, one-loop resistor network with declared signs, then interpret any negative current physically.

controlled_variation.hold: the physical circuit and component values
controlled_variation.notice: solutions change sign with the reference choice but predict the same physical current directions

controlled_variation.hold: the same circuit and branch-current references
controlled_variation.notice: every loop term reverses consistently and the conservation statement is unchanged

family.invariant_demand: Read the circuit topology, choose the applicable element model, write conservation constraints, solve for the requested current or voltage, and check the result against charge and energy conservation.
family.difficult_move: Translating the drawing into the correct shared-quantity and conservation constraints before doing algebra.
family.independent_check: At every junction the signed currents sum to zero, and for a closed steady network the source power and resistor dissipation are consistent with the solved values.

support_ladder.handed_over: Branch directions, node labels, and the first applicable element relation are supplied.
Node labels and a suggested loop are supplied, but the learner chooses signs and equations.
Only the circuit, component values, and requested quantity are supplied.

transfer.changed_demand: Replace one resistor with a filament or diode-like element whose V-I graph is non-linear and decide which circuit relations remain valid.
transfer.information_not_handed_over: whether a single constant resistance is a valid model for that element

transfer.changed_demand: Given an I-V graph plus a node-network diagram, determine the operating current and voltage.
transfer.information_not_handed_over: which graphical operating point satisfies the circuit constraint

transfer.changed_demand: Analyze a sensor circuit described in words rather than with familiar resistor labels.
transfer.information_not_handed_over: which physical parts map to source, branch, and resistive element roles

transfer.changed_demand: After solving a mixed series-parallel network, determine whether a resistor exceeds a stated power rating.
transfer.information_not_handed_over: the need to carry the solved branch current or voltage into a separate power check
